report.headline: Usage projected to drop to 13.8% from 16.9% in the G League, about 1.2 standard deviations below the NBA's 20.0% average, while the true-shooting projection is not trustworthy for this transition.

projection.text: The model projects a 13.8% usage rate in the NBA, down from 16.9% in the source G League season, roughly 1.2 standard deviations below the target league's average of 20.0%.

risks.text: The true-shooting projection of 53.7% carries no real information: the model's error (4.7%) is matched exactly by a trivial league-average baseline, so this number should not be used to judge scoring efficiency.
Central usage projection of 13.8% is below the NBA average of 20.0% by more than one standard deviation (5.3%), implying a reduced offensive role relative to the receiving league's typical player.

The estimate rests on only 45 historical G League to NBA transitions, and this player's standing above their own league (+0.27 sd) was modest compared to typical movers, adding to the uncertainty of any single projection.

The 95% interval for usage (5.7% to 21.8%) covers more than three standard deviations of the NBA usage distribution, underscoring that any point estimate should be read as a wide range rather than a precise forecast.

strengths.text: In the source season the subject produced 15.2 points per 75 possessions on a 61.6% true shooting mark, 1.10 standard deviations above the G League average.
Shot selection was heavily three-point oriented (42.8% of attempts) alongside a low 9.4% turnover rate.
The upper end of the 80% usage interval (19.0%) sits close to the NBA average of 20.0%, leaving room for a full-role outcome if the projection lands high.

uncertainty.text: The 80% prediction interval for usage runs from 8.5% to 19.0% and the 95% interval from 5.7% to 21.8%, spans wide enough relative to the league's 5.3-point standard deviation that the model can rank this transition but not pin a precise value; separately, the true-shooting projection of 53.7% should not be treated as informative because its held-out error (4.7%) is no better than simply guessing the league average (4.7%).
